newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Contraband pouring through SAfrican airfields - paper.
newsitem.headline: Contraband pouring through SAfrican airfields - paper.

text.p: Soviet-made cargo planes and light aircraft are landing illegally at South African airports, bringing in illegal immigrants and ferrying out contraband such as stolen cars, police told a Sunday newspaper.
The Sunday Independent quoted detectives as saying that some of the aircraft were used by international crime rings run by Russians, Ukrainians and other East Europeans.

"We are investigating the Russian mafia for the theft of luxury cars like BMWs and Mercedes-Benzes in South Africa," Captain Giacomo Bondesio, of the police's crime syndicate investigations unit, told the paper.
"The engine numbers are changed so the cars can be resold here and in neighbouring countries."

Home Affairs sources told the paper South African intelligence agents have been monitoring expatriates from former Iron Curtain countries now resident in the country. They said some may be former KGB secret-service operatives now involved in the crime rings.

Several Soviet-built cargo planes of various sizes are operating in South Africa, chartered by local or foreign companies. They fly mainly to the rest of Africa and can operate from rudimentary or uncontrolled airstrips, aviation industry sources said.
Superintendent Piet Smit of the border police unit told The Sunday Independent large-scale smuggling could take place because the radar system was inadequate.
He said the system operated only in well-defined "corridors" and air smugglers aware of them could easily fly undetected through South African air space.
Another problem is the lack of sophisticated equipment to scan crates and containers.

More than 200 licensed aiports and aerodromes are dotted around the country. Peter Hattingh, of the civil aviation department, said only major airports were properly controlled by immigration and customs officials.
An international airport in the north of the country has been ordered to turn off its runway landing lights at night after a number of alleged illegal landings.
